newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hard for Japan to protect bank debentures--Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Hard for Japan to protect bank debentures--Moody's.

text.p: Japan's deposit insurance system would face difficulties in protecting holders of bank debentures issued by three long-term credit banks if one of the banks defaulted, Moody's Investors Service said.
Nippon Credit Bank Ltd (NCB), the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd and the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan Ltd are Japan's main issuers of bank debentures.
"Use of the system's resources for the protection of the three long-term credit banks' debenture holders may be very difficult," Moody's said in a report issued on Tuesday.

The leading credit rating company said bank debentures are uninsured and consequently the three long-term credit banks' insurance premium payments are much lower than those of other banks. It also said any discrimination between bank debenture holders and other corporate bond holders was not justified under current laws.

The Japanese financial authorities' stance on the issue is that a failure among the long-term credit banks is extremely unlikely, and that therefore they do not need the system's resources, Moody's said.

Moody's warned, however, that in a stress situation, institutional investors could be forced to suffer in one way or another, such as maturity extension, interest reduction or conversion into other securities. Moody's said it defines such "distressed exchanges" as defaults.
Domestic bank debentures serve as an important long-term savings tool for both institutional and individual investors.

Moody's said it had some concerns about procedures to resolve any large bank failure, partly because the problem was much bigger than the Japanese authorities realised. Resources available for the Deposit Insurance Corp (DIC) appear insufficient to protect senior creditors of large Japanese banks, it added.
Moody's said a current shift in the industry to market discipline and accounting transparency may eventually expose certain creditors of banks rated E or E+ to risk.
"We expect that the banks rated E+ or E may ultimately require official assistance," it said in the report.

It has assigned its E+ financial strength rating to six Japanese banks, including Hokkaido Bank Ltd and Hokuriku Bank Ltd. Its E ratings, the lowest ones, have been assigned to four Japanese banks including NCB and Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd.
